sections.title: Counting What the Loop Repeats
sections.body:
To name a function's complexity you do not time it - you count how many times its **innermost work** happens as a function of the input size $n$. Work that happens a fixed number of times no matter how big the input gets is **constant time**, written $O(1)$: reading `a[0]` costs the same on ten elements as on ten million.

A single loop that visits every element once does its body $n$ times, so it is **linear**, $O(n)$. The reliable move is to put a counter in the body and watch the counter, because the counter is the thing the notation is about.

What matters is the **shape of the loop bound**, not the body. A body that does five additions instead of one still runs $n$ times, and $5n$ and $n$ belong to the same class.

annotations.text: No loop, no recursion: one indexing operation. This is O(1) - the input could be a billion long.
The loop bound is a.length, so the body runs exactly n times. This bound is the whole story.
The counter is the honest measure. Watch it, not the wall clock.
Ten times the input, ten times the steps: 10 then 100. That straight-line relationship is what O(n) means.

checkpoint.explain: The counter ends at the array's length because the loop bound is the array's length - that is exactly why the first print grows with the input and the second one does not. Indexing `items[0]` is one operation on an array of 6 or 6 million, which is the difference between O(n) and O(1) made concrete.

sections.title: Loops Inside Loops Multiply
sections.body:
When one loop sits inside another, the inner body runs once for **every pair** of outer and inner steps, so the counts **multiply**: $n$ outer passes times $n$ inner passes is $n^2$. Doubling the input therefore quadruples the work, which is the signature of **quadratic time**, $O(n^2)$.

A triangular nesting - where the inner loop starts at `i + 1` and so shortens each pass - runs $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ times. That is half of $n^2$ minus a linear term, and it is still $O(n^2)$: the constant $\frac{1}{2}$ does not change how the curve bends.

The rule to read off the page is short. **Nested loops over the same $n$ multiply, and the exponent is the nesting depth.**

annotations.text: This inner loop restarts from 0 on every outer pass, so it runs n times, n times over.
Starting at i + 1 shortens the inner loop every pass: n(n-1)/2 steps in total.
25, 100, 400 - squaring the input size, exactly as n^2 predicts.
Doubling n multiplied the work by 4. That factor of 4 is the fingerprint of a quadratic.

checkpoint.prompt: Give the time complexity of `hasDuplicate(a)` in terms of `n = a.length`, and justify it by counting the comparisons in the worst case.
checkpoint.explain: In the worst case - no duplicate at all - the comparison runs once for every unordered pair, which is n(n-1)/2 times. That is half a square minus a linear term, and both the 1/2 and the -n/2 are discarded, leaving O(n^2). The early `return true` only helps some inputs, and a complexity class is named by the worst case, not by the lucky one.

sections.title: Halving Gives You a Logarithm
sections.body:
A loop that **cuts the remaining work in half** each pass cannot run $n$ times, because after $k$ halvings only $n / 2^k$ is left. Solving $n / 2^k = 1$ gives $k = \log_2 n$, so the loop runs about $\log_2 n$ times and the function is $O(\log n)$.

That is a startlingly flat curve: a million items need about 20 passes, a billion about 30. The base is left out of the notation because changing base only multiplies by a constant - $\log_2 n$ and $\log_{10} n$ differ by a fixed factor of about 3.32.

The pattern to recognise is **the loop variable being divided or multiplied**, not incremented. `i = i / 2` and `i = i * 2` both give $\log n$ passes, while `i = i + 1` gives $n$.

annotations.text: The loop variable is divided, not decremented. That single character is what makes this logarithmic.
0, 1, 3, 9, 19 steps. A million-fold jump in n costs 19 passes, not a million.
Math.floor keeps the value a whole number, and it strictly decreases while above 1 - which is why the loop terminates.
20 -> 10 -> 5 -> 2 -> 1: five passes for n = 40, and 2^5 = 32 is just under 40.

checkpoint.prompt: Trace `let i = 100;` under `while (i > 1) { i = Math.floor(i / 2); }`. Give the value of `i` after each pass, then the total number of passes.
checkpoint.explain: Six passes for n = 100, and $\log_2 100 \approx 6.64$ - the floor division rounds the count down. Notice how cheap a hundred elements are, and that the flooring at pass 3 (25 becomes 12, not 12.5) never threatens termination, because the value strictly decreases on every single pass.

sections.title: Adding, Dropping and the Dominant Term
sections.body:
Two loops **one after another** do not multiply - their counts **add**. Two passes over the same array is $n + n = 2n$ steps, and $2n$ is $O(n)$, because a constant multiplier does not change the shape of the curve.

When the added pieces have different shapes you keep only the **dominant term**: $n^2 + n$ is $O(n^2)$, since for large $n$ the square swamps everything under it. So $3n^2 + 50n + 700$ is $O(n^2)$ too, however large that 700 looks at $n = 5$.

Two rules finish the floor.

- **Sequential work adds; nested work multiplies.**
- **Drop constant factors, and drop every term but the fastest-growing one.**

annotations.text: ...plus n * n from this one. They are sequential, so the counts add: n^2 + n in total.
The ratio to n^2 marches 1.1000, 1.0100, 1.0010 towards 1. The linear term is being swallowed.

checkpoint.prompt: A function does exactly $3n^2 + 50n + 700$ operations. Explain why it is $O(n^2)$, and why that is still the right answer even though $50n + 700$ is far bigger than $3n^2$ when $n = 5$.
checkpoint.explain: Big-O describes behaviour as $n$ grows without bound, not at any one small size. Past about $n = 30$ the quadratic term takes the lead and keeps pulling further ahead, so the lower-order terms and the factor 3 change only where the curve sits, never how it bends. Naming the class is about the shape of growth; the constants belong to benchmarking.

guided-practice.explain: Counting is the primitive skill under every complexity claim: one loop gives n, the same loop nested inside itself gives n times n. Six and thirty-six are not just two numbers here - they are the two growth classes you are learning to tell apart at a glance.

guided-practice.prompt: Name the time complexity of `secondLargest(a)` in terms of `n = a.length`, and justify it by counting how many array elements the function inspects and how much work each one costs.
guided-practice.explain: A branching body is still a constant amount of work per element - at most two comparisons and two assignments - so the loop bound alone decides the class. This is the trap the floor is training away: complexity counts how many times a body runs, not how many lines are inside it.

guided-practice.prompt:
Trace `steps` in this triangular nesting for `n = 4`, starting from `steps = 0`. Give the value of `steps` at the end of each outer pass.

`for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) { steps++; } }`
guided-practice.explain: The inner loop shrinks by one each pass - 3, then 2, then 1, then 0 - and 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 6 = n(n-1)/2. Watching the increments die away shows exactly where the factor of one half comes from, and why half a square is still a square.

guided-practice.prompt: Fill the blanks so this loop runs in $O(\log n)$ time: it must keep going while `i` is above 1, and shrink `i` by a factor of two on each pass.
guided-practice.explain: Dividing rather than decrementing is the single edit that turns a linear loop into a logarithmic one, and the `> 1` guard is what makes it terminate: `i` strictly decreases while it is above 1, so the loop cannot run forever. Writing `i - 2` in place of the division would give n/2 passes, which is still O(n).

guided-practice.prompt: Write `innerSteps(n)` returning how many times the innermost line runs in `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) { /* here */ } }`. It must return `0` for `n = 0` and for `n = 1`.
guided-practice.hint: Either simulate the loops, or use n * (n - 1) / 2 - and check the two agree at n = 5.
guided-practice.explain: Both accepted answers - the simulation and `n * (n - 1) / 2` - produce identical numbers, which is the point: the closed form is what the nested loops *are*, and it is where the n^2 in O(n^2) becomes visible. The n = 0 and n = 1 cases matter because a loop that never enters still has a well-defined cost of zero.

guided-practice.prompt: Two functions both process an array of length `n`. One runs two separate loops one after the other; the other runs one loop nested inside another. Explain why the first is $O(n)$ and the second is $O(n^2)$.
guided-practice.explain: Sequential loops finish one before the other starts, so their counts add: n + n = 2n, and the 2 is a constant factor that drops away. A nested loop restarts its whole run for every outer step, so the counts multiply into n * n. The layout on the page - side by side, or one inside the other - is what decides between addition and multiplication.

guided-practice.prompt: Put these complexity classes in order from slowest-growing to fastest-growing.
guided-practice.explain: The ordering is what makes the classes useful: at n = 1,000,000 these cost roughly 1 step, 20 steps, a million steps and a million million steps. Constant beats logarithmic beats linear beats quadratic for every large enough n, which is precisely why the dominant term is the only one worth naming.

exam.prompt: Name the time complexity of `middleThree(a)` in terms of `n = a.length` and justify it.
exam.explain: Reaching the middle of an array is not the same as walking to it: indexing is a single address computation, so three reads cost three steps whatever the length. Constant time means the step count contains no `n` at all - not that the function is short.

exam.prompt: Name the time complexity of `countDigits(n)` for a positive integer `n`, and justify it in terms of how `n` changes on each pass.
exam.explain: Dividing by 10 rather than 2 gives $\log_{10} n$ passes, and $\log_{10} n$ is $\log_2 n$ divided by about 3.32 - a constant factor, which big-O discards, so the base never appears in the notation. Any loop whose variable is divided by a fixed constant greater than 1 is logarithmic.

exam.prompt: Name the time complexity of `report(a)` in terms of `n = a.length`. Your justification must account for both loops.
exam.explain: The two phases are sequential, so their costs add to $n^2 + n$, and then the linear term is dropped because the square dominates it for all large $n$. Deleting the first loop entirely would not change the answer - which is the practical lesson: optimising anything but the dominant term buys nothing asymptotically.

Multiplying up to n is the mirror image of halving down from it and gives the same count: `i` takes the values 1, 2, 4 for n = 8, stopping when it reaches 8. Eight times the input cost three more passes rather than eight times as many - that is $\log_2$ read straight off the output.

exam.prompt: Trace a binary search over the 16 indices `0..15` where the target always lies in the upper half of whatever range remains. Start with `lo = 0`, `hi = 15`; each pass computes `mid = Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2)` and then sets `lo = mid + 1`. Give `lo,hi` after each pass, then the number of passes until `lo > hi`.
exam.explain: The window width goes 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, 0 - halving each pass - so sixteen candidates are exhausted in five looks rather than sixteen. The halving is also the termination argument: a width that strictly shrinks and cannot go below zero must reach zero, so the loop provably ends.

exam.prompt: Write `halvingSteps(n)` returning how many times `n` can be replaced by `Math.floor(n / 2)` before it reaches 1 or below. `halvingSteps(1)` is `0` and `halvingSteps(8)` is `3`.
exam.explain: The function you just wrote *is* $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, computed by a loop instead of a formula, and the counts it returns - 19 for a million - are why $O(\log n)$ is treated as almost free. `n = 1` returning 0 is the edge case proving the loop is guarded at the top rather than run at least once.

exam.prompt: Someone claims that `for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 2) { ... }` is $O(\log n)$ because it "skips half the work". Explain what is really happening and give the correct class.
exam.explain: Halving the work **once** is a constant factor; halving the **remaining** work on every pass is a logarithm. This loop runs n/2 times, and n/2 is O(n) - doubling n still doubles the cost, which a logarithmic loop never does. The tell is that `i` is incremented by a constant rather than divided by one.

exam.prompt: Two loops run one after another over the same array of length `n`. Complete the accounting: first the total step count as a multiple of `n`, then the complexity class, writing only what goes inside the brackets of `O(...)`.
exam.explain: Writing the count down before naming the class is the discipline that stops guesswork: 2n really is twice the work of n, yet both are straight lines, so both are O(n). Constants matter to a stopwatch and not to a growth class.

exam.prompt: Which of these runs in $O(n^2)$ time, where `n = a.length`?
choices: for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { for (let j = 0; j < 10; j++) { total++; } }
for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { for (let j = 0; j < a.length; j++) { total++; } }
for (let i = 1; i < a.length; i = i * 2) { total++; }
for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { total++; } for (let j = 0; j < a.length; j++) { total++; }
exam.explain: Only the second nests one n-bounded loop inside another. The first is nested but its inner bound is the constant 10, giving 10n = O(n); the third doubles its counter, giving O(log n); the fourth is sequential, giving 2n = O(n). Nesting alone does not make a quadratic - both bounds have to depend on n.

exam.prompt: Select every statement that is true of $f(n) = 4n^2 + 1000n + 9$.
choices: It is O(n), because 1000n is the largest term when n = 10.
The constant 9 is dropped because it does not grow with n.
The factor 4 is dropped because a constant multiplier does not change the growth class.
It cannot be bounded by n^3, since f has no cubic term.
exam.explain: Big-O is a claim about large $n$, so which term is biggest at $n = 10$ is irrelevant - that is the classic error in the second option. The last option is false too: $O$ is an upper bound, so this function genuinely is $O(n^3)$ as well; $O(n^2)$ is simply the tightest bound, and the tightest one is what we mean when we name a class.
